extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, newsroom editors and educators
extracted.subtask_description: A field‑level code of ethics and criteria for news judgment describing moral duties, procedural limits (e.g., suppression), and qualitative standards (accuracy, independence, humanity) that should guide journalists and news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public journal as a public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: "I believe that the public journal is a public trust."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism exists to serve the public; stories and editorial decisions must be justified as serving that public trust rather than private or sectional interests. Use the public‑trust test when deciding whether to publish or withhold material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear thinking, clear statement, accuracy and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: "I believe that clear thinking, clear statement, accuracy and fairness are fundamental to good journalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should be lucid, factually accurate, and balanced. Avoid vague phrasing, sloppy verification, and unfair presentation of opposing views. These four elements are presented as foundational—failure on any undercuts journalistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth / personal conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: "I believe that a journalist should write only what he holds in his heart to be true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should not publish claims they do not genuinely believe to be true; this emphasizes moral conviction and personal accountability for published content. Anti‑pattern: repeating or amplifying falsehoods for clicks or pressure when the reporter does not believe them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression only for the welfare of society
rubrics_metrics.description: "I believe that suppression of the news, for any consideration other than the welfare of society, is indefensible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding news is only permissible to protect society's welfare (for example, to prevent imminent harm). Suppression for political, commercial, or personal considerations is condemned. Use a narrow, defensible standard when deciding to suppress information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bribery and conflicts of interest; gentlemanly conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "I believe that no one should write as a journalist what he would not say as a gentleman; that bribery by one's own pocketbook is as much to be avoided as bribery by the pocketbook of another."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must avoid accepting payments, gifts, or other inducements that compromise integrity; they should behave with the civility and honesty they would show in personal life. Disclosure and recusal are implied remedies for conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from pride, opinion, and greed of power
rubrics_metrics.description: "...is stoutly independent, unmoved by pride of opinion or greed of power..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and newsrooms should resist influence from powerful interests, ideological pride, or financial incentives. Independence includes editorial autonomy and resisting censorship or co‑optation by wealthy/privileged actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive journalism and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "...constructive, tolerant but never careless, self‑controlled, patient..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism should seek to build understanding and solutions rather than merely sensationalize; be tolerant and open to perspectives, but exercise care, restraint, and patience in reporting. Avoid irresponsibly provocative or reckless reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful yet unafraid; quick indignation at injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: "...always respectful of its readers but always unafraid, is quickly indignant at injustice..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain respectful tone toward audiences while being willing to confront wrongdoing and injustice vigorously. Courage to report uncomfortable truths is a duty; disrespectful or fear‑driven silence is an anti‑pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unswayed by privilege or the clamor of the mob
rubrics_metrics.description: "...is unswayed by the appeal of privilege or the clamor of the mob..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bias toward elite interests and avoid following crowd sentiment uncritically. Journalists should evaluate claims on evidence and principle rather than rank, pressure, or popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give every person a chance; promote equal opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: "...seeks to give every man a chance, and, as far as law and honest wage and recognition of human brotherhood can make it so, an equal chance..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should aim to provide voice and opportunity across society, not privilege certain groups. Strive for inclusive reporting that highlights barriers to equality and provides fair access to platform and scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotic while promoting international goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: "...is profoundly patriotic while sincerely promoting international good will and cementing world‑comradeship..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance national loyalty with a global conscience: report in ways that serve the nation's interests without denouncing international cooperation or empathy. Avoid jingoism that undermines objective reporting about other nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism of humanity and present relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: "...is a journalism of humanity, of and for today's world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center human dignity and contemporary relevance in coverage. Stories should illuminate lived human experience and address issues pertinent to current society rather than abstruse or purely sensational matters divorced from public concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust as a justification for stories (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: public_trust — use public trust as justification for any story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating newsworthiness, ask whether the story serves the public trust. Avoid pursuing items of curiosity or commercial value that do not advance the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welfare of society test for suppression (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: welfare_of_society — suppression is only defensible to protect society's welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a societal‑welfare standard narrowly when considering non‑publication (e.g., imminent harm). Do not use supposed 'welfare' as a pretext for protecting powerful interests or concealing wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice orientation (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: justice — journalism should be 'quickly indignant at injustice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize exposing and explaining injustice; let a concern for fairness and redress shape reporting choices and investigative priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction over destruction (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: construction — prefer constructive reporting rather than destructive sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to inform and improve civic life; avoid reporting styles aimed solely at tearing down individuals or institutions without public‑interest justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance over sectarianism (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: tolerance — favor tolerance rather than sectarianism in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report with openness to differing viewpoints and avoid amplifying sectarian or divisive framings that inflame social division without informative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to contemporary audience (implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit criterion: today's world — stories should relate to present concerns and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stories for topical relevance and their usefulness to a contemporary public; prioritize reporting that helps audiences navigate current events and civic choices.
